It is a surprisingly sharp, layered detective story that uses its colorful, sprawling animal metropolis to tackle some pretty heavy themes without ever feeling preachy. The chemistry between the cynical, street-smart Nick and the relentlessly optimistic Judy is the heart of the movie, making their partnership feel earned and genuinely funny. Visually, the world-building is top-tier-every district of the city feels unique and lived-in, from the tiny rodent-sized streets to the massive rainforest canopy. While the central mystery is engaging and keeps you guessing, it's the clever social commentary and the way it subverts typical "follow your dreams" tropes that makes it a modern classic. It is a rare animated film that manages to be equally hilarious for kids and incredibly thoughtful for adults.
An entertaining movie with a heartwarming moral for the little ones. A real mystery for young and old alike!

"Zootopia" turns out to be a truly entertaining buddy cop action comedy in animated form, one that is extremely creative thanks to its premise and, toward the end, also strikes some genuinely good socially critical notes that are seamlessly woven into the plot.

I really liked the attention to detail in the design of "Zootopia" and how all the different species are integrated into the city. The pop culture references were also funny. What I liked best was how the characters were portrayed... I especially liked the scene where a character, after a long day, hesitates to answer her parents' call because she's afraid of having to put on a happy face. That was very relatable.
The highlight is definitely the sloth scene at the registration office (DMV): It playfully subverts the well-known cliché of the sluggish bureaucrat.
Conclusion: A good story that's well told. Lots of attention to detail and humor. The characters are well written and, I dare say, portrayed "realistically."

Uneven Execution in Action and storytelling

Dune: Part Two is epic science fiction in its purest, most uncompromising form: a film that excels across every cinematic dimension. From its masterful direction to its breathtaking cinematography, from its immersive sound design to its razor-sharp editing, this is filmmaking operating at the highest level.

Dune: Part Two builds on the foundation of its predecessor with remarkable confidence and scale. Denis Villeneuve crafts a world that feels both grand and intimate, balancing spectacle with emotional depth in a way few modern blockbusters manage. Every frame is deliberate, every sequence purposeful.

At the heart of it all is Timothée Chalamet, who delivers a career-defining performance as Paul Atreides. He captures the internal conflict of a young man burdened by destiny torn between personal identity and the weight of prophecy. His transformation feels earned, gradual, and deeply human.

The supporting cast is equally exceptional. Each actor, no matter how much screen time they have, plays their role to perfection. Whether it's seasoned performers commanding major arcs or those appearing briefly yet leaving a lasting impression, the film maintains a consistent level of excellence throughout.

What makes this adaptation especially powerful is its respect for Frank Herbert's original vision. The film translates complex themes into a cinematic language that is both accessible and profound. It never feels watered down, nor does it overwhelm; instead, it trusts the audience.

The pacing is deliberate but never sluggish, allowing tension to build organically. The action sequences are visually stunning without sacrificing clarity or emotional stakes. Combined with its haunting score and meticulously crafted world-building, the film becomes an experience rather than just a story.
From its literary roots to the smallest on-screen performance, everything about this film feels meticulously crafted.

Entertaining in the Moment, Forgettable by Morning

Nobody is the kind of film that feels designed for a casual evening watch. You click on it, watch it, and move on. That is not necessarily a crime, but it also defines the film's biggest limitation. It never rises above being "fine." In many ways, it feels like Nobody, the movie, because once it ends, it leaves almost no trace in your memory.

The story feels loosely inspired by the John Wick template. An underestimated man with a violent past is pulled back into action, unleashing controlled chaos. Some elements clearly echo that formula, while others feel randomly stitched together. The result is a plot that technically functions, but lacks cohesion and purpose. Nothing about it feels particularly thought-out beyond the basic setup.

At just over ninety minutes, the short runtime is noticeable. The film moves quickly, but not in a way that feels tight or efficient. Instead, it feels thin. Ideas are introduced and resolved without much development, and the narrative never has space to breathe. Rather than benefiting from its brevity, the film feels undercooked.

The action is easily the strongest component. The fight choreography is solid, the gunplay is punchy, and the weapon handling has a satisfying physicality. None of the action is revolutionary, but it is competently staged and consistently watchable. The problem is that the film does not offer much beyond that. Unlike visually spectacular films where style alone can carry the experience, Nobody does not have a strong enough identity to compensate for its weak storytelling.

Character engagement is minimal. Bob Odenkirk is excellent in Better Call Saul and Breaking Bad, but here his performance feels restrained in a way that never becomes compelling. He is not bad, but he does not elevate the material either. Most of the supporting cast leaves little impression, which makes it hard to care about anyone's fate.

Christopher Lloyd's appearance is a small highlight, and his presence injects a bit of personality into the film. Similarly, the way weapons are used and presented has a certain tactile charm that adds to the fun of the action scenes.

Ultimately, Nobody is not offensive, embarrassing, or actively frustrating. It is simply empty. It is the kind of movie you watch when it shows up on your streaming homepage, finish without regret, and then immediately forget. In that sense, it truly earns its name. It is Nobody, the film.

a gripping, unflinching dive into the shadowy world of the U.S.-Mexico border drug war

Sicario (2015) is a gripping, unflinching dive into the shadowy world of the U. S.-Mexico border drug war, directed with masterful tension by Denis Villeneuve. Emily Blunt shines as Kate Macer, an FBI agent thrust into a morally ambiguous task force that's equal parts thrilling and terrifying. Her performance grounds the film in raw vulnerability, making her the perfect audience surrogate as she navigates a labyrinth of secrets and violence.

The supporting cast elevates it further-Josh Brolin brings a charismatic, enigmatic edge to his CIA operative, while Benicio del Toro delivers a haunting, understated portrayal that's both chilling and profoundly human. Roger Deakins' cinematography is nothing short of breathtaking, capturing the desolate landscapes and high-stakes action sequences with a visceral intensity that keeps you on the edge of your seat. The score by Jóhann Jóhannsson pulses with dread, amplifying the film's exploration of ethical gray areas and the cost of unchecked power.

While it doesn't reinvent the thriller genre, Sicario excels in its taut pacing and thought-provoking themes, leaving a lasting impact without resorting to cheap shocks. It's a smart, stylish film that rewards multiple viewings.
Rating: 8/10.

The Heat is on
Heat is an utterly brilliant police procedural crime thriller, packed to the gills with incredible action sequences, technical brilliance, and shockingly nuanced dramatic tensions.

The acting from across the board amongst the ensemble cast is simply more phenomenal than could ever be expected; Al Pacino and Robert De Niro virtually play two sides of the same coin as workaholics, in their own ways. Whereas Pacino's Vincent is written to be more clearly lost in his personal life and only ever feels found when he is working, De Niro's Neil has the added layer of being aware that his line of work is not one to be considered socially acceptable. Interwoven with intelligent dialogues and clever writing, it creates a uniquely fascinating divide that both unites and separates the leads, making them both equally flawed and compelling and moreso influencing the audience to root for the antagonists just as much as the protagonists, even despite the former being on the wrong side of the law. Moreover, the large set pieces and wide shots used to capture them creates an immersively large scale that leads to fantastic mappings out of action scenes; the shoot-out choreography is kept track of beautifully with minimal editing cuts, leading to the geography of scenes being captured easily, clearly and coherently. And again, it is all through the awe-inspiring cinematography that also manages to uplift the rest of the film as well from the furthest skyline shots to the closest dramatic close-ups.

On the other hand, however, the movie is admittedly close to perfection but can restrict itself from a certain point of view. There are several side plots the film forms, and it naturally builds out the world to be highly detailed and more lived-in. One such fantastic example is the relationship between Val Kilmer and Ashley Judd, showing the more damaged and toxic drawbacks to living a life of crime in an effectively moving way. But another example is Vincent's troubled stepdaughter played by Natalie Portman. She provides another aspect of how complex and loaded Vincent's personal life is, but also feels so rightfully pushed aside that the overall runtime needed more or less of her; she never really contributes much until one of the final sequences of the film and yet she's in enough of the movie that she should feel more involved and emotionally deep than she ends up coming across. But admittedly, her few scenes balance the pacing, and more scenes could have thrown off the movie and made the side story feel more like a glaring distraction.

In conclusion, Heat is perhaps the closest a film of its calibre can get to being a flawless masterpiece. Following through on demonstrating the efficiency of both cops and crooks, and never failing to make it feel dangerously exciting.

It is a surprisingly sharp, layered detective story that uses its colorful, sprawling animal metropolis to tackle some pretty heavy themes without ever feeling preachy. The chemistry between the cynical, street-smart Nick and the relentlessly optimistic Judy is the heart of the movie, making their partnership feel earned and genuinely funny. Visually, the world-building is top-tier-every district of the city feels unique and lived-in, from the tiny rodent-sized streets to the massive rainforest canopy. While the central mystery is engaging and keeps you guessing, it's the clever social commentary and the way it subverts typical "follow your dreams" tropes that makes it a modern classic. It is a rare animated film that manages to be equally hilarious for kids and incredibly thoughtful for adults.
An entertaining movie with a heartwarming moral for the little ones. A real mystery for young and old alike!

"Zootopia" turns out to be a truly entertaining buddy cop action comedy in animated form, one that is extremely creative thanks to its premise and, toward the end, also strikes some genuinely good socially critical notes that are seamlessly woven into the plot.

I really liked the attention to detail in the design of "Zootopia" and how all the different species are integrated into the city. The pop culture references were also funny. What I liked best was how the characters were portrayed... I especially liked the scene where a character, after a long day, hesitates to answer her parents' call because she's afraid of having to put on a happy face. That was very relatable.
The highlight is definitely the sloth scene at the registration office (DMV): It playfully subverts the well-known cliché of the sluggish bureaucrat.
Conclusion: A good story that's well told. Lots of attention to detail and humor. The characters are well written and, I dare say, portrayed "realistically."

This Is Where I Leave You wants to be a sharp, heartfelt family drama. It ends up as a smug, self-satisfied mess.

The film mistakes constant talking for insight. Characters ramble endlessly but reveal very little, recycling tired observations about grief, marriage and adulthood without saying anything new. Every emotional beat is undercut by a joke that isn't funny, as if the film is afraid of sincerity.

The ensemble cast is wasted on thin, unlikeable characters who feel written to showcase wit rather than humanity. Their privilege is never interrogated, only indulged. Pain is cosmetic, growth is implied rather than earned, and conflict resolves because the script says it should, not because the characters change.
Worst of all, the film treats family dysfunction as a quirky aesthetic instead of something real. It gestures at depth, then backs away, settling for sentimentality and snark.

By the end, This Is Where I Leave You feels less like a reflection on loss and more like a two-hour therapy session you didn't consent to - self-absorbed, shallow, and convinced of its own importance without doing the work to deserve it.

Guy Ritchie's The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare is one of those rare war films that refuses to follow the usual formula-and that's exactly what makes it so entertaining. Inspired by a real covert British unit during World War II, the film delivers explosive action, clever strategy, and a refreshing dose of humor.

What makes the movie stand out is its tone. Instead of being overly grim like many war films, it embraces a stylish, almost rebellious energy. The characters feel larger than life, yet their camaraderie and confidence make them incredibly fun to watch. The humor lands naturally, often in the middle of intense situations, which keeps the pacing lively and unpredictable.

The action sequences are slick and well choreographed, and Guy Ritchie's signature style-sharp editing, cool music choices, and confident storytelling-is present throughout the film. At the same time, the suspense never disappears, because the missions always feel risky and daring.
Overall, The Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare is an outstanding mix of action, humor, and suspense. It's bold, stylish, and incredibly entertaining from start to finish.
A blast, sillier and more stylised than you'd expect from a based on true story WW2 movie

As long as you go in knowing vaguely what to expect, you will have a lot of fun with Ministry of Ungentlemanly Warfare. Is it a masterpiece? Once Upon a Time... in Bloatwood: Tarantino's Three-Hour Ego Trip to Nowhere

Oh, where do I even begin with Quentin Tarantino's excruciatingly bloated, shamelessly self-indulgent, and endlessly masturbatory love letter to the fading glory days of 1969 Hollywood? This cinematic endurance test clocks in at a punishing 161 minutes-yes, you read that correctly, two hours and forty-one minutes of what feels like the director's personal scrapbook dumped onto the screen without a single thought given to pacing, narrative economy, or the poor souls unfortunate enough to sit through it in a theater. It's the kind of movie that makes you check your watch every ten minutes, wondering if the projectionist accidentally spliced in footage from three different abandoned projects and called it a day. If your idea of entertainment is being trapped in a car with your rambling grandpa who insists on recounting every single irrelevant detail of his youth while you desperately search for an exit ramp that never comes, then congratulations: this is the film for you. For everyone else with a functioning attention span and a shred of self-respect, prepare to suffer through what can only be described as a vanity project so bloated it could sink the Titanic all over again.

Let's talk about the so-called "stars" at the center of this meandering mess. Leonardo DiCaprio and Brad Pitt are undeniably gifted actors, and on paper, their chemistry should be electric. In practice, though? They're essentially coasting on autopilot, riding the wave of their established star power and effortless good looks while the script gives them next to nothing substantial to do. DiCaprio's character, a fading Western TV star named Rick Dalton, spends what feels like an eternity flubbing lines on set, throwing tantrums in his trailer, and staring wistfully at old movie posters-all while the camera lingers on every bead of sweat and every dramatic sigh as if we're supposed to find profound pathos in a washed-up actor's midlife crisis. Pitt, playing his stunt double and best buddy Cliff Booth, fares slightly better in the charisma department, but even he's reduced to a series of repetitive, oddly fetishized chores: fixing a roof here, driving a vintage Cadillac there, wandering around Los Angeles in search of nothing in particular. Their banter is cute for about fifteen minutes, but when that's stretched across nearly three hours with zero actual plot momentum, it stops feeling like charming camaraderie and starts feeling like filler-pure, unadulterated padding designed to let Tarantino indulge his obsession with 1960s cars, neon signs, and vintage clothing catalogs.

And don't even get me started on the film's so-called "central conflict," which is dangled in front of the audience like a shiny carrot for the first two hours before being unceremoniously slaughtered in one of the most tasteless, cartoonishly over-the-top, and downright offensive fantasy sequences ever committed to celluloid. The Sharon Tate and Charles Manson angle is teased relentlessly-Margot Robbie's Tate is shown floating through Hollywood like a ethereal dream girl, barefoot and beaming, while ominous hints of the Manson Family lurk in the background like cheap horror-movie foreshadowing. We're led to believe this might actually say something meaningful about the death of innocence, the end of an era, or the collision between celebrity glamour and real-world violence. Instead, Tarantino pulls a cheap alternate-history rug out from under us with a flamethrower-wielding, blood-soaked climax that turns genuine historical tragedy into a smug, self-satisfied spectacle of cartoon violence. It's not clever. It's not subversive. It's not even darkly humorous. It's just Tarantino jerking himself off in public, high on his own nostalgia and convinced that rewriting history with gallons of fake blood makes him some kind of edgy genius. What should have been a poignant tribute to a real-life loss becomes an empty, nihilistic middle finger to anyone who came expecting emotional depth, historical respect, or-God forbid-actual stakes.

Speaking of Margot Robbie: her role as Sharon Tate is an absolute criminal waste of talent. She's given maybe twenty minutes of screen time total, during which she mostly smiles beatifically, wanders barefoot through bookstores, watches herself on screen at a theater, and radiates effortless beauty while contributing precisely zero to the plot. It's the cinematic equivalent of hiring a world-class chef and then asking them to just stand in the kitchen looking pretty while someone else burns the meal. The film treats her like a decorative prop in Tarantino's rose-tinted vision of old Hollywood, reducing one of the era's most tragic and iconic figures to a series of glossy, fetishized vignettes. If you're going to build an entire marketing campaign around "the women of Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood," at least give them something to do besides serving as eye candy for the director's personal fantasy reel.

The dialogue? Ninety percent of it is little more than Tarantino's favorite party trick: endless, winking name-dropping of obscure 1960s TV shows, forgotten B-movies, and vintage Hollywood trivia that only the most obsessive film buffs could possibly care about. Characters don't converse; they recite Wikipedia entries about forgotten Westerns and radio jingles while the audience is expected to nod along in reverent recognition. It reeks of the worst kind of boomer nostalgia-the kind that romanticizes a bygone era without ever bothering to interrogate its flaws, its hypocrisies, or its very real darkness. Instead of substance, we get surface-level fetishization: vinyl records spinning, cigarettes dangling from lips, muscle cars cruising down Sunset Boulevard. It's all style and no soul, a hollow celebration of "when movies were movies" delivered by a director who seems to believe his own hype so completely that he forgot to write an actual story.

In the end, Once Upon a Time... in Hollywood isn't just disappointing; it's actively insulting to anyone who values tight storytelling, genuine emotion, or basic respect for historical sensitivity. If you're in the mood to watch two aging Hollywood icons drive around Los Angeles while Quentin Tarantino indulges every single one of his signature fetishes-feet, violence, pop-culture masturbation, and vintage cars-then by all means, knock yourself out. But for the love of cinema, the rest of us should spare ourselves the agony and simply rewatch Pulp Fiction instead. At least that film knew how to tell a story without turning into a three-hour ego trip. This one? Skip it. Life is too short for such empty, overlong, self-congratulatory nonsense.

I found Anora, its cast, and Mikey Madison absolutely remarkable. I have always been drawn to films that feel lived in, especially New York stories or anything that captures the grit, contradictions, and unpredictability of real life rather than leaning on polished, Hollywood contrivance. This film does exactly that, and it does it with confidence.

What struck me most is how human it feels. The characters are not reduced to types or devices to move a plot along. They breathe, they react, they contradict themselves, and they exist in a world that does not bend to make things easier for them. Not everything is a transaction, and the film understands that in a way that feels honest rather than sentimental. There is humor that comes naturally out of situations, moments that are uncomfortable in a truthful way, and an emotional undercurrent that builds without forcing itself on the audience.

The performances are exceptional across the board, grounded and unforced. Mikey Madison, in particular, delivers something that feels fearless and fully committed. There is no sense of "acting" in the traditional way. It feels observed, inhabited, and real. That kind of performance is not easy to pull off, and it elevates everything around it.

There is also a rhythm to the film that trusts the audience. It does not over-explain, it does not clean things up to make them more digestible, and it does not rely on spectacle to hold attention. Instead, it leans into behavior, dialogue, and consequence. That restraint gives it weight.

This was more than just a pleasant surprise. It reminded me why films like this matter. When storytelling is grounded in truth and performances are this strong, you do not need big names or manufactured moments. You just need honesty, and this film has it.
Undoubtedly, a fairy tale

I'm struck by statements like "it's not a typical fairy tale." Because it is, and above all, it's a distorted, rose-tinted portrayal of the world of prostitution. I doubt that sex workers can afford to alternate lap dance sessions with pleasant chitchatting with colleagues over a cigarette. I wish a sex worker's life were so enviable, but I am afraid that they are not.

So, once again, we fall into the trap of movies, of which Anora is an example, showing us a distorted reality that is what most of the public wants to see. And I would be happy if those who offer their opinions would refrain from adding the caveat that "it's not your typical fairy tale." Having overcome this hurdle, and finally speaking about Anora, it must be said that the film is entertaining and well-paced. The actors and actresses, as well as the sets (Coney Island, Brighton Beach, etc.), the cinematography, the editing, and the color grading, are all well done and contribute to a pleasant viewing experience.

Best Picture, Best Director, Best Actress, Best Supporting Actor, Best Original Screenplay? I wouldn't agree, but it's well known that the Oscars© reward what the Academy members consider good for the public and suitable for all audiences. Ultimately, it won 5 Oscars.
A Modern Fairy Tale with Intense Emotions

Anora presents a modern fairy tale that explores just how long a lie can last. Mikey Madison delivers an impressive range of emotions from start to finish, conveying them to the audience in a genuine way. Watching her extreme happiness crumble in an instant highlights how easily people can manipulate each other, a point made even clearer across different social classes. While the story drags a bit before the final resolution, Anora evokes a variety of strong feelings, culminating in an intense ending that underscores the disregard some upper-class individuals have for those less privileged, and contrasts a loving man with a spoiled boy.

Godfather

The Godfather, directed by Francis Ford Coppola, is widely considered one of the greatest films ever made, and for good reason. The movie tells the story of the powerful Corleone crime family and explores themes of power, loyalty, family, and the corrupting nature of authority. While it is often categorized as a gangster film, it goes far beyond that genre and becomes a deep character study about how power shapes people and relationships.

One of the film's greatest strengths is its characters. Marlon Brando delivers a legendary performance as Don Vito Corleone, the aging patriarch of the family. His calm voice, slow movements, and controlled authority make the character feel both intimidating and strangely honorable. At the same time, Al Pacino gives an incredible performance as Michael Corleone, the youngest son who initially wants nothing to do with the family's criminal empire. Watching Michael slowly transform from a quiet war hero into a ruthless mafia leader is one of the most fascinating character arcs in cinema.

The film's storytelling is patient and deliberate. Instead of relying on constant action, it builds tension through dialogue, relationships, and carefully structured scenes. Moments like the opening wedding sequence or the quiet conversations between family members allow the audience to fully understand the world of the Corleones. When violence finally appears, it feels shocking and meaningful rather than simply entertaining.

Visually, the movie is also remarkable. The cinematography by Gordon Willis uses dark lighting and shadow to create a moody and powerful atmosphere that reflects the secretive nature of organized crime. The music composed by Nino Rota is equally memorable, with its haunting main theme becoming one of the most recognizable scores in film history.

The reason I would rate this film a 9/10 instead of a perfect score is mainly because its slow pacing may feel challenging for some viewers, especially modern audiences used to faster storytelling. However, that same pacing is also part of what gives the film its depth and realism.

Overall, The Godfather is a masterclass in filmmaking. With outstanding performances, powerful themes, and unforgettable moments, it remains one of the most influential movies ever made and a must-watch for anyone interested in cinema.

The nature of the tale has clear links to the soap opera genre, and the explicit themes are both simple and inherently anti-intellectual (Tom Hagen is the counterweight in this respect - until he is deemed surplus to requirements). And yet these two features might just be deciding factors for the initial success and subsequent consolidation of The Godfather as one of the most renowned and acclaimed films in the history of cinema. Francis Ford Coppola demonstrates that the key is meeting the demands of the public with storytelling of gargantuan proportions. He structures his film as a classical epic, adds a well-measured amount of pulp, and executes it all with brilliant craftsmanship - both in front of and behind the camera. One of Coppola's greatest achievements here is the parallel between the 1940s family story he tells and how the same mechanisms still operate in a broader political context today. As a period piece, The Godfather is accurate, charming, and visually striking. It looks better and has more detail than most gangster films set in the same era. Furthermore, the film deals devotedly with the Italian/American connection, and the segments from Sicily not only spice up the film, but also function as a fine thematic backdrop for the rest of the story.

What ultimately makes The Godfather so effective is the thoroughness in the storytelling, the strength of the characters, and how both these aspects are anchored to perfection in the classic tragedy. Rarely has a wider variation of tragic flaws been presented at once on film. And carried by a diverse range of characters, they call on great performances. Marlon Brando, as so often during this period of his career, approaches his role with an aloofness that borders on caricature. This time, however, it is a pinpointed caricature elevated by his magnetic command, and as the film unfolds, the character seems to grow on him. Few things are more fascinating than watching Brando when he fully embodies a character - when he loses himself in it. The scene with Don Vito's grandson is absolutely captivating. Al Pacino's performance is notable for its metamorphosis. He grows into a compelling figure that typifies Pacino's subsequent career. Yet in many ways, Pacino is at his best in the early parts of the film. The final of the three best performances belongs to Robert Duvall, whose subdued, sensitive Tom Hagen represents a notable contrast to the other members of the family. A family that fascinates and frustrates, reaching you with its all-encompassing, extreme nature - partly shared by some of the most capitalistic Western societies (including the United States) today.

Films by director Christopher Nolan tend reach for something interesting, and I doubt anyone would accuse him of a lack of ambition. Sometimes that pays off, sometimes it doesn't. But like the saying goes, even if you fail it shows you tried. Many directors don't even try, or don't get the leeway from their financial backers to try.

To start with the positives, there are some wonderful shots in this film. The approach to Saturn is a classic, and the black hole is wonderful in its sheer violence (even if the special effects get notably stretched). The actors all delivered, some in spades: Matthew McConaughey (Cooper) and Mackenzie Foy (young Murph) are particularly convincing here. Anne Hathaway (Brand) has solid moments in the middle of the film, but unfortunately gets sidelined. The way the story weaves into itself is generally well done. I also didn't mind the soundtrack by Hans Zimmer here, and consider that praise. For all his undisputed technical skills, I just don't share his preferences when it comes to film soundtracks.

Some cons that make me reluctant to rate it higher: the film is way too long, and there are several scenes that could have been cut as they rehash things already established. Without getting into spoilers, the uninhabitable prospects the crew explores are extremely unoriginal. I won't fault the film for falling into the trap of making the universe seem small, as its scale might just be something that humans cannot comprehend. But it is more of an issue when it comes to Earth itself, where the film struggles to credibly juggle a post-population-collapse society (which happened at most a decade or two ago) with high-tech secret government agencies using technologies far in advance of what is possible today. Which, of course, only exist in the United States. Obviously.

But all of that are minor quibbles compared to the ending. We spend over two and a half hours following Cooper getting somewhere, and then wrap the story up in like 10 minutes in the most cheesy way possible. And it is stitched together with fade-to-black moments that are beneath a director like Nolan. Throughout, the film tries so hard to be profound, but it never dares to commit: not to the (false) choices it teases, and not to any lasting personal tragedy. In this context I will also mention, but otherwise ignore, the awkwardness of pushing the same poem unto the audience three or four different times.
To wrap up, this film is undoubtedly a visual spectacle, well made and acted, but is let down by a lacklustre plot that eventually succumbs to a tired 'love conquers all' cliche. Worth seeing once.

Dune: Part Two is epic science fiction in its purest, most uncompromising form: a film that excels across every cinematic dimension. From its masterful direction to its breathtaking cinematography, from its immersive sound design to its razor-sharp editing, this is filmmaking operating at the highest level.

Dune: Part Two builds on the foundation of its predecessor with remarkable confidence and scale. Denis Villeneuve crafts a world that feels both grand and intimate, balancing spectacle with emotional depth in a way few modern blockbusters manage. Every frame is deliberate, every sequence purposeful.

At the heart of it all is Timothée Chalamet, who delivers a career-defining performance as Paul Atreides. He captures the internal conflict of a young man burdened by destiny torn between personal identity and the weight of prophecy. His transformation feels earned, gradual, and deeply human.

The supporting cast is equally exceptional. Each actor, no matter how much screen time they have, plays their role to perfection. Whether it's seasoned performers commanding major arcs or those appearing briefly yet leaving a lasting impression, the film maintains a consistent level of excellence throughout.

What makes this adaptation especially powerful is its respect for Frank Herbert's original vision. The film translates complex themes into a cinematic language that is both accessible and profound. It never feels watered down, nor does it overwhelm; instead, it trusts the audience.

The pacing is deliberate but never sluggish, allowing tension to build organically. The action sequences are visually stunning without sacrificing clarity or emotional stakes. Combined with its haunting score and meticulously crafted world-building, the film becomes an experience rather than just a story.
From its literary roots to the smallest on-screen performance, everything about this film feels meticulously crafted.

Nobody is the kind of film that feels designed for a casual evening watch. You click on it, watch it, and move on. That is not necessarily a crime, but it also defines the film's biggest limitation. It never rises above being "fine." In many ways, it feels like Nobody, the movie, because once it ends, it leaves almost no trace in your memory.

The story feels loosely inspired by the John Wick template. An underestimated man with a violent past is pulled back into action, unleashing controlled chaos. Some elements clearly echo that formula, while others feel randomly stitched together. The result is a plot that technically functions, but lacks cohesion and purpose. Nothing about it feels particularly thought-out beyond the basic setup.

At just over ninety minutes, the short runtime is noticeable. The film moves quickly, but not in a way that feels tight or efficient. Instead, it feels thin. Ideas are introduced and resolved without much development, and the narrative never has space to breathe. Rather than benefiting from its brevity, the film feels undercooked.

The action is easily the strongest component. The fight choreography is solid, the gunplay is punchy, and the weapon handling has a satisfying physicality. None of the action is revolutionary, but it is competently staged and consistently watchable. The problem is that the film does not offer much beyond that. Unlike visually spectacular films where style alone can carry the experience, Nobody does not have a strong enough identity to compensate for its weak storytelling.

Character engagement is minimal. Bob Odenkirk is excellent in Better Call Saul and Breaking Bad, but here his performance feels restrained in a way that never becomes compelling. He is not bad, but he does not elevate the material either. Most of the supporting cast leaves little impression, which makes it hard to care about anyone's fate.

Christopher Lloyd's appearance is a small highlight, and his presence injects a bit of personality into the film. Similarly, the way weapons are used and presented has a certain tactile charm that adds to the fun of the action scenes.

Ultimately, Nobody is not offensive, embarrassing, or actively frustrating. It is simply empty. It is the kind of movie you watch when it shows up on your streaming homepage, finish without regret, and then immediately forget. In that sense, it truly earns its name. It is Nobody, the film.

Friday The 13th As Pastiche.
Ah, yes.
The legendary classic which started it all.
Who would have thought it would go on to spawn a dozen films.
After introducing one of the most classic horror movie characters of alltime...
...Without ever actually introducing him.
As a standlone slasher, it's quite good.
Possessing an amount of gore that was unrivalled by it's predecessors.
Effectively setting the standard for the future of slasher films, through the rest of the 80s...and beyond.
What this film did different, though, is that it paid hommage to all the great films- and cases- that inspired it.
For example, Pamela Voorhess is quite clearly based on Hitchcock's archetypal killer from Psycho.
Having mimicked the psychology of Norman Bates...while simultaneously reversing the scenario...so as to keep things "original".
Which is kind of genius, when you think about it.
Likewise, the part where Pamela smashes through the door with an Axe clearly pays hommage to Kubrick's iconic scene from The Shining.
While the style in which the film is shot (ie from the perspective of the unseen killer) harkens back to the infamous Canadian slasher Black Christmas.
You can also see the influence that Argento had on the film, in the way that Miller & Cunningham maintained the air of mystery, around the identity of the killer.
Not to mention the way in which the burgeoning sexuality of the characters play into the plot...though, in a much more repressed, Americanized, way (compared to it's European giallo counterparts).
And you can't deny that Hooper's equally iconic character, Leatherface, influenced the physical appearance of Jason (in that both are deformed).
But that's not all.
Keep in mind that both Bates and Leatherface were inspired by real life serial killer Ed Gein.
Cunningham gives a nod to this at the very beginning of the film, with the truck driver who drove Annie to the crossroads by Camp Crystal Lake.
Other serial killer references spun into the film include, the whole "Hitchhiker Murder" trope (alluded to by the first killing).
The Zodiac Killer's signature...which can be seen on the Seneca cabin's nameplate, right before Brenda's murder.
And Steve Christy (the owner of Camp Crystal Lake)...who totally gives off Edmund Kemper (the Co-Ed Serial Killer) vibes.
You could even go as far as arguing that the blue Jeeps, here, play a similar role to the Volkswagon Bugs of Ted Bundy (cough cough...Part 3).
But that might be pushing it.
Either way...when you consider all of above...you've really got to appreciate Friday The 13th for being a rather clever pastiche.
As it did- for the films before it- what Scream would later do for the generation of films it would go on to inspire.
Making it, not just a classic in it's own right...but a film designed to recognize it's predecessors.
Which is what makes it truly great, in my opinion.

The other thing that keeps the audience interested is the incredible central performances from Jodie Foster and Anthony Hopkins, with Foster being the main point of alignment with a subtle and composed performance which hides a distinct feeling of fear.

And no wonder she's scared, because Hopkins is absolutely terrifying, playing a composed yet maniacal killer which has spawned many copies over the years. But one must also acknowledge the fact that his whole performance is enhanced by the camerawork being from the perspective of Clarice when POVs from her are presented. Seriously scary stuff.
Quick note, the supporting cast is equally watertight.
The storyline is incredibly solid. Like a jigsaw puzzle with no pieces missing, and the editing is nothing short of iconic, you know what sequence I'm talking about.
But one thing which I was astounded by was the score. Howard Shore manages to conjure a sense of dread and tenacity along with a whole host of emotions in it.

I am tentative to give this film a 10/10 because I don't believe it was perfect, but let me tell you, this film was not far off. My only qualm would be that at times, the film felt self indulgent, but that is merely a personal criticism which doesn't strip the film of any of its glory.
If you haven't already watched this film, do yourself a favour...

2008(5.0) I watched Scary Movie 2 in 2008, and it remains a visceral 5.0-star pillar of comedic anarchy in my archive-a raw revelation of how a stagnant horror genre could be dismantled by a narrative rhythm that felt 100% chewy and sensational. This experience shattered the fourth wall of the supernatural thriller by infusing the Wayans brothers' raw, unapologetic absurdity into a rhythmic journey that turned every pathetic trope into a vivid act of storytelling rebellion. The narrative rhythm was far from stagnant; it offered a sensational barrage of high-tension slapstick-from the raw, iconic butler with the tiny hand to the vivid but pathetic struggle with the possessed cat-leaving me in a state of absolute joy at the sheer chewy wit of the subversion. Seeing the vivid parody of The Exorcist and The Haunting provided an emotional payoff that felt both raw and sensational, proving that an obsession with low-brow humor could achieve a permanent, sensational scar of brilliance on my soul. The 95% preservation of my memory is dominated by the rhythmic, raw brilliance of the dinner scene and the vivid but pathetic desperation of the characters trapped in the mansion, creating a journey that felt like a definitive masterpiece of the absurd. Unlike the stagnant 1.0-star drift of Home Alone 4, this encounter possessed a rebellious soul that turned every pathetic cliché into a sensational artifact of wit. It stands in my 2008 record as a powerful 5.0-star testament to the raw power of parody-a high-tension encounter with the vivid rhythm of the ridiculous that remains one of the most chewy artifacts of my cinematic journey.
A Notable Downgrade from the Original

Unfortunately, the sequel feels like a significant step down. The pacing is off, and it takes far too long for the plot to find its footing. While there are a few specific standout gags, most of the humor feels dated and forced-which is surprising considering the first film still feels fresh. It lacks the sharp writing of the predecessor and relies too heavily on shock value that hasn't aged well. A watchable but mediocre 5/10.

Anna Faris, Regina Hall and Shawn Wayans still give good performances that go all in once again. Christopher Masterson and Kathleen Robertson are equally committed new additions however, David Cross is easily the strongest one who gets some of the best moments. Marlon Wayans getting more screen time in this one is definitely an easy win and one of the only aspects it's able to improve over the superior first instalment.

The Scary Movie version of Ghostface who got plenty of laughs previously is definitely missed here but returning director Keenen Ivory Wayans still finds inventive ways to deliver fun sequences and clever visual gags which don't repeat themselves too often, even if they arrive less frequently. Also, the extended opening that parodies The Exorcist with an almost overwhelming amount of bodily fluids is a really effective way to set the tone.

Half-Baked but Thrilling

28 Days Later is a tense and distinctive entry in the zombie and post-apocalyptic genre. The film does a great job of creating a sense of isolation, anxiety, and constant threat through the empty streets of London, and parts of its survival narrative are genuinely gripping. The direction feels different and occasionally bold, which helps the film stand apart from similar works.

That said, the film clearly suffers from storytelling issues. The screenplay struggles not only with narrative structure and pacing, but also with logical consistency. Many of the characters' decisions in an apocalyptic survival situation lack credibility, and the story rarely offers fresh or compelling ideas, which weakens several key moments.

The low image quality, although an intentional creative choice, ends up hurting the film. This visual weakness reduces the impact of certain scenes, despite the moody atmosphere the film tries to establish.
The ending, even if designed to allow for continuation, doesn't feel particularly logical or convincing.
Overall, 28 Days Later is bold and creative, but its narrative, logical, and visual shortcomings prevent it from reaching its full potential. My rating: 6-7/10.

Profoundly Entertaining and Wildly Disturbing!

American Psycho is probably one of the strangest movies I've ever seen. I've seen it a few times and I have to say, I think I finally understand it. It is meant to have an ambiguous ending, because as Bateman's final line goes, "this confession has meant nothing." It's a critique on the lack of meaning, lack of morality, and complete and utter ignorance and disregard of 1980s yuppie culture and political mania. It is taken to an extreme, but the film does a great job of displaying the emptiness of a man's life and soul, and how his surroundings and circumstances have influenced his nature. Whether he committed the murders or not, either way, he is using it as a means of escape and a means of fulfilling the emptiness within. Bateman feels like it gives him purpose or, at least, something to run toward. The movie has so many clues that point to what it all really means, which is nothing. That's the point. It's all about shallow thinking and emptiness of the soul. The satirical nature of the film makes for excellent entertainment, but there are definitely moments that are questionable. As a whole, it's a film that is hard to ignore, and it does have some flaws, but it is definitely worth watching at least once.

Sinopsis: En una ciudad de animales antropomórficos, una conejita policía y un cínico zorro estafador forman equipo para desvelar una conspiración.
Reseñas: One of my favourite Disney movie

It is a surprisingly sharp, layered detective story that uses its colorful, sprawling animal metropolis to tackle some pretty heavy themes without ever feeling preachy. The chemistry between the cynical, street-smart Nick and the relentlessly optimistic Judy is the heart of the movie, making their partnership feel earned and genuinely funny. Visually, the world-building is top-tier-every district of the city feels unique and lived-in, from the tiny rodent-sized streets to the massive rainforest canopy. While the central mystery is engaging and keeps you guessing, it's the clever social commentary and the way it subverts typical "follow your dreams" tropes that makes it a modern classic. It is a rare animated film that manages to be equally hilarious for kids and incredibly thoughtful for adults.
An entertaining movie with a heartwarming moral for the little ones. A real mystery for young and old alike!

"Zootopia" turns out to be a truly entertaining buddy cop action comedy in animated form, one that is extremely creative thanks to its premise and, toward the end, also strikes some genuinely good socially critical notes that are seamlessly woven into the plot.

I really liked the attention to detail in the design of "Zootopia" and how all the different species are integrated into the city. The pop culture references were also funny. What I liked best was how the characters were portrayed... I especially liked the scene where a character, after a long day, hesitates to answer her parents' call because she's afraid of having to put on a happy face. That was very relatable.
The highlight is definitely the sloth scene at the registration office (DMV): It playfully subverts the well-known cliché of the sluggish bureaucrat.
Conclusion: A good story that's well told. Lots of attention to detail and humor. The characters are well written and, I dare say, portrayed "realistically."

Zootopia is an entertaining animated film that blends humor, action, and a thoughtful message in a very accessible way. The world-building is impressive, creating a vibrant city where different animal species coexist, each with their own lifestyles and personalities. The animation is colorful and lively, and the voice performances add a lot of charm to the characters.

What makes the movie stand out is how it touches on themes like stereotypes, ambition, and understanding others while still keeping things light and enjoyable. The story moves at a good pace and keeps you engaged with a mix of comedy and mystery elements.

While it may feel slightly predictable at times, it remains a fun watch with plenty of clever moments and heart. Overall, Zootopia is a solid animated film that works for both kids and adults, offering laughs and a positive message along the way.

Perhaps because Nintendo has meant so much to me, since I was 8 years old, I put off watching "The Super Mario Bros. Movie" due to fears of the film not living up to my hopes. With the sequel imminent though, I decided that it was time to give it a go. It doesn't tarnish the legacy but also isn't at the top tier of animated films.

Italian American plumbers Mario (Chris Pratt) and Luigi (Charlie Day) are transported to a parallel universe, the Mushroom Kingdom. The Kingdom is ruled by benevolent Princess Peach (Anna Taylor-Joy). However, Bowser (Jack Black) King of the Koopas conquers the nearby Snow Kingdom to claim a prize, with the aim of presenting the Star to Peach as a token of his unrequited love.

I liked the attention to detail in the film. From the very beginning there are plenty of references to games both within and adjacent to the Mario series. I liked how the references the side scrolling platforming aspects of the games at various points too. Chris Pratt came in for some criticism for his Mario voice at the time of the films release, but if I'm honest it's fine, and I didn't rub up against it.

I will say that perhaps the story is thin. You might argue that the film is primarily for kids, but it doesn't come close to the emotional explorations of something like "Toy Story" or "Inside Out". Despite the fun references too it doesn't really come close to the humour style of "The Lego Movie" either.
But let's not go overboard, I did think the film was alright and now I've seen this one I'm on board to see "The Super Mario Galaxy Movie" in the next couple of weeks.

Reseñas: A Visually Stunning Take on the Spider-Man Universe

Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse stands out as one of the most visually unique superhero films in recent years. The animation style feels like a living comic book, full of vibrant colors, creative transitions, and energetic action sequences that make the entire movie feel fresh and dynamic.

The story introduces a new Spider-Man while expanding the universe in a fun and imaginative way. The characters are likable, the humor lands well, and the film does a great job balancing emotional moments with fast-paced superhero action. The soundtrack and overall vibe also add a lot to the film's personality.

At times the story can feel a bit familiar if you've seen other Spider-Man films, but the creativity in presentation keeps things engaging. Overall, it's a stylish and entertaining superhero movie that brings something different to the genre.
Best animation in a film
Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse is an outstanding film. From the story to the visuals and the soundtrack, every part of it works together to create something truly special.

The story itself is incredibly entertaining. Watching all the different Spider people come together to face a massive lineup of villains is exciting from beginning to end. At the center of it all is Miles Morales' journey, which is both emotional and inspiring. His growth throughout the film feels genuine, and the famous "leap of faith" moment stands out as one of the most powerful scenes in the entire movie. It perfectly captures the heart of his character and the message of the story. The writing is sharp, heartfelt, and consistently engaging.

While the story is excellent, what truly elevates this film is its groundbreaking animation. The movie manages to bring together multiple completely different animation styles. Each style is tied to a different Spider character, yet they blend together seamlessly in the same scenes. It is visually stunning and incredibly creative. The story follows Remy, a rat with an extraordinary sense of taste and smell who dreams of becoming a chef in Paris. Despite the obvious obstacles-his species being unwelcome in kitchens-Remy refuses to give up on his passion. This central conflict makes the film deeply engaging, as it explores what it means to pursue a dream in a world that seems determined to reject you. The message that "anyone can cook" is not about literal cooking ability, but about the idea that talent and creativity can come from the most unexpected places.

The attention to detail in the animation is extraordinary, especially in the food itself. Every dish looks vivid and mouthwatering, making the culinary world feel alive. Super

Through Ego's perspective, Ratatouille examines the role of critics and the courage it takes to create something new. It suggests that while criticism can be harsh, it is also an essential part of artistic growth. This adds a level of sophistication that appeals to both younger audiences and adults.

Music plays a key role in enhancing the film's atmosphere. The score, composed by Michael Giacchino, perfectly captures the spirit of Paris and the emotional tone of the story. The soundtrack is light, whimsical, and occasionally dramatic, complementing the narrative without overpowering it.

Sinopsis: Jake Sully vive con su nueva familia en el planeta de Pandora. Cuando una amenaza conocida regresa, Jake debe trabajar con Neytiri y el ejército de la raza na'vi para proteger su planeta.
Reseñas: The Sequel That Dives Even Deeper
Directed once again by James Cameron, Avatar: The Way of Water proves that lightning can strike twice. Honestly, this one is just as good as the original - and in some ways, I might even prefer it.

Let's start with what absolutely works: the visuals are on another level. If the first Avatar pushed CGI forward, this one perfects it. The underwater performance capture is stunning. The oceans of Pandora feel alive - every ripple, creature, and coral reef looks breathtakingly real. Cameron doesn't just show you the water; he immerses you in it.

What really surprised me, though, was the emotional core. This film leans heavily into family - Jake and Neytiri as parents, their children finding their identities, and the tension that comes with protecting the ones you love. The Sully family dynamic adds weight to the action. The stakes feel more personal this time around.

That said, this movie definitely has more problems than the first. The biggest one? Length. The Way of Water feels like it could have easily been split into two films. Certain stretches - especially in the middle - linger longer than they need to. Some scenes could have been trimmed without losing impact. The pacing occasionally slows the momentum, and you feel every minute of the runtime.

But even with those issues, I can't deny how much I enjoyed it. The action sequences are intense and beautifully shot. The score (building on the legacy of James Horner's original themes) blends emotion and scale perfectly. And thematically, this film feels deeper - exploring belonging, survival, and generational legacy.
Is it flawless? No. It's long, indulgent at times, and occasionally repetitive. But it's also bold, beautiful, and emotionally stronger in many ways than the first.
In my opinion, this might actually be my favorite over the original.
